title: Potted Beef
subtitle: Slow-braised beef shredded in spiced butter, served on toast
excerpt: Potted beef is a British preserve-and-eat dish: beef slow-braised until it falls apart, then shredded finely and packed into pots with spiced butter, which sets around the meat and keeps it for up to five days. It is eaten cold, spread thickly on hot toast, and is one of the most satisfying things you can keep in the fridge.
sourceNotes: Potted meats have been part of British food culture since at least the seventeenth century as a method of preserving cooked meat under a butter seal. Potted beef was particularly common in the Victorian era and appears in domestic manuals and cookery books of the period. Modern versions use the refrigerator rather than relying on the butter for preservation.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and keep refrigerated for up to 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 2 hours ahead to set. Lasts 5 days in the fridge.

content.text: Potted beef is the British answer to rillettes or pate de campagne: a long-braised meat, broken down and preserved under fat. The spices (mace, cayenne, and a touch of nutmeg) give it a Victorian warmth that separates it from a plain cold roast. The shredded beef can be processed very fine (almost smooth) or left in visible strands. Both are correct depending on preference.

Heat the oven to 150°C fan. Season the beef generously. Place in a small Dutch oven with {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, the bay leaves, and thyme. The stock should come about halfway up the beef. Cover tightly and braise for 3 hours until the beef is falling apart.
Remove the beef and leave to cool. Strain the braising liquid and reduce on the hob to about 4 tablespoons of concentrated, glossy stock. Cool.

Shred the cooled beef finely with two forks, removing any sinew. Mix with {{unsalted-butter}} of softened butter, the reduced braising stock, the mace, cayenne, nutmeg, and {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Season well. Taste: it should be highly seasoned.
Pack tightly into small pots or ramekins. Melt a little extra butter and pour over the top to seal. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours until set. Serve at room temperature, spread on hot toast.

items.cause: Insufficient seasoning or spices, or the Worcestershire sauce was omitted.
items.fix: Potted beef must be very well seasoned , more than seems right before potting. The fat mutes flavours as it sets. The spices should be clearly present.

items.symptom: The texture is greasy rather than spreadable
items.cause: Too much butter relative to meat.
items.fix: The ratio should be roughly 1 part butter to 5 parts meat. The butter should coat and bind, not dominate.

items.symptom: The beef has not shredded finely enough and is still in chunks
items.cause: The braise was not long enough, or the beef was not rested before shredding.
items.fix: Braise for the full 3 hours. The beef should shred with almost no effort using two forks. If it still resists, return to the oven for 30 more minutes.

items.symptom: The butter seal has not set firm
items.cause: The pots were filled while still warm.
items.fix: Cool the potted beef completely before pouring the butter seal over. A warm mixture will not give a clean solid seal.

content.text: Potted beef was a Victorian household staple, made from leftover roast or slow-braised cuts. The butter seal kept the meat for several days before refrigeration existed. The spiced version became popular because the butter absorbs the mace and cayenne over time and the flavour deepens. As a modern dish it is one of the best things to keep in the fridge. It takes time to make and almost no effort to eat, and it is better than most shop-bought pate on a piece of hot toast.
